content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: In running totals and moving averages, define the unit of analysis before writing the query: one row per customer, order, day, or other grain. Make filters, NULL handling, time boundaries, and tie-breaking rules visible in the SQL.

items.title: Cumulative sums
items.text: Cumulative sums summarizes rows. Decide the grain of the result first, group only by the dimensions that define one output row, and verify NULL and duplicate behavior in each metric.

items.title: Moving averages
items.text: Moving averages is easier to reason about when the input row grain, partition keys, ordering, and tie-breaking rule are explicit. A window expression can add a calculation while keeping the individual input rows visible.

items.title: Period-to-date calculations
items.text: Period-to-date calculations needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Choosing suitable window frames
items.text: Choosing suitable window frames is easier to reason about when the input row grain, partition keys, ordering, and tie-breaking rule are explicit. A window expression can add a calculation while keeping the individual input rows visible.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT order_date::date AS order_day,
       SUM(total_amount) AS daily_revenue,
       SUM(SUM(total_amount)) OVER (ORDER BY order_date::date) AS running_revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY order_date::date
ORDER BY order_day;
content_blocks.expected_output: The output has one row per observed day and a running revenue total across the ordered dates. Add a unique ordering key if multiple rows can share the same date before windowing.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
